turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brought you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Dr. ____, I’m here because... well, it’s a long story, but for almost two years now, I’ve been dealing with this situation that I just cannot shake, and it's completely exhausting me. I’m a music director and a composer, and right after this major commission I had—which was supposed to be this huge, positive turning point for me after finishing my graduate degree—things just took a turn. 

I have this absolute certainty, and I mean I know it in my bones, that a few specific people in the ensemble started quietly working together to undermine my work. And they don't do it out in the open where I can just stop the baton and address it. It’s all these incredibly calculated, subtle things. They’ll use sudden schedule changes that just happen to rob us of the most critical rehearsal time for my pieces, or they'll make these very specific seating choices that completely ruin the acoustic balance I'm trying to build in the string section. And then there are these little comments... just these tiny, quiet remarks during rehearsals that are designed to throw off my focus or undermine my authority with the rest of the players. 

And the most frustrating part, the reason my head feels like it's spinning all the time, is that whenever I try to bring it up, they have these perfect excuses ready to go. They’ll actually pull up emails or forward me administrative notes that supposedly explain why the rehearsal room was double-booked, or why the seating chart had to be adjusted for spacing, as if that proves it was all just an innocent clerical error. But I know what I'm seeing. You don't just accidentally sabotage a director's work for almost two years straight. No matter how much supposed proof or documentation they show me, I know exactly what they are doing to me, and it's making it nearly impossible to do my job.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses an absolute, unshakeable certainty that ensemble members are conspiring to undermine their work, maintaining this belief even when presented with contradictory evidence like emails and administrative notes.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices that other people could not hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? No, no, definitely not. I mean... well, as a composer, obviously my head is always full of sound, right? Like, if I'm working on a new orchestration, I can close my eyes and hear the brass section coming in, or I can hear the exact timbre of the cellos against the violas. That's just part of the training, part of the job. You have to be able to audiate the score before you ever step onto the podium. 

And sure, lately, I do find myself replaying the things those specific ensemble members have said to me—like, over and over again when I'm alone in my apartment, trying to parse out exactly what they meant by a certain inflection when they claimed the rehearsal room was booked. I'll just sit there and loop their excuses in my head, analyzing the tone of their voices from earlier that day, trying to catch the exact moment they decided to lie to me. But it's just my memory, you know? It's just me thinking and analyzing the situation because I have to be ten steps ahead of them. 

I'm not sitting here hearing phantom people talking to me out of thin air or anything like that. My hearing is actually incredibly sharp, which is probably why I pick up on all their little whispered comments during rehearsal in the first place when they think I'm focused on the woodwinds. I hear exactly what is actually there, in the room. So no, no imaginary voices.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient exhibits paranoid and persecutory ideation, believing ensemble members are lying to him, plotting against him, and whispering about him behind his back.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing imaginary voices or phantom people, clarifying that the sounds in his head are just his musical audiation and memories.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe this group is specifically targeting you because of a special message, power, or outside force that no one else can perceive?
turns.patient_response:
A special message? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, there’s no outside force or... or mystical power at play here. It’s actually incredibly mundane, which in a way makes it even more infuriating. It’s just pure, calculated, professional jealousy and resentment. 

You see, when I got that commission right out of my graduate program—and this was a highly competitive commission, mind you, the kind that usually goes to someone who has been in the industry for at least a decade—it ruffled a lot of feathers. People in the ensemble, especially these specific older players who have been sitting in the exact same chairs playing the exact same repertoire for fifteen years, they really didn't like taking direction from a twenty-six-year-old. They didn't like that I came in with fresh ideas and demanded a much higher level of precision than they were used to giving. 

So it's not about a special message or me having some kind of supernatural ability or anything like that. It's just about power dynamics in the rehearsal room. They want to maintain their comfort zone, and my presence, my success with that commission, directly threatens that. So they decided to tear me down, piece by piece, starting with the acoustics and the scheduling, like I mentioned. It’s entirely human, incredibly petty, and entirely grounded in the reality of orchestral politics. 

I mean, if you've ever spent time in a professional music organization, you'd know how vicious the politics can get, but this... this is taking it to a level I never anticipated. They don't need an outside force to be vindictive, they just need an ego and a willingness to ruin a good piece of music just to put me in my place. So, no, no special powers or secret messages. Just very real, very deliberate, very exhausting sabotage.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, detailed belief that the ensemble is deliberately and systematically sabotaging their work due to professional jealousy, which is indicative of persecutory delusions.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any other experiences where you felt things were clearly affecting you that other people said were not real?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I haven't. I mean, everything I'm experiencing, everything I'm telling you about, it's all completely grounded in reality. It's just that other people aren't paying attention, or they're willfully ignoring it because it's easier to just go along with the status quo than to admit that there's a concerted effort to undermine someone. 

Like, take the administration, for example. I've tried to explain to the operations manager how these "accidental" double-bookings always seem to happen on the days I'm premiering a new movement, and he just brushes it off. He'll say, "Oh, you know how the scheduling software is, it's just a glitch," or "We're just really tight on space this season." He tells me it's not real, that I'm just stressed about the music. But he's not the one standing on the podium, looking at half an empty room because the brass section was supposedly told rehearsal started an hour later. 

So it's not that I'm experiencing things that aren't real, it's that I'm experiencing things that are incredibly real, and the people around me are either too blind to see the pattern or they're just making excuses for the people doing it. I don't have... I don't have visions or hallucinations or anything bizarre like that. Everything I see is actually happening. The emails are real, the empty chairs are real, the ruined acoustics are real. It's just their interpretation of it—or their refusal to see the malice behind it—that differs from mine. They want to call it a series of unfortunate coincidences. I know it's deliberate sabotage. But outside of this specific situation with the ensemble? No, nothing like that. My life outside of this job is perfectly normal. It's just this one, incredibly toxic professional environment that's completely draining me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed, unyielding belief that they are being deliberately sabotaged by colleagues, despite others providing rational explanations like software glitches.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies experiencing hallucinations, stating they do not have visions or see things that aren't there.

turns.doctor_question: How certain are you that this group is sabotaging you—could you be wrong?
turns.patient_response:
Could I be wrong? No, I... I mean, I'm here, aren't I? I'm talking to you because for almost two years now, I've been completely unable to shake this certainty. It's not a passing thought, it's a reality I live with every single day. I'm absolutely certain that after I got that commission, a few specific people in the ensemble just... they made a decision. They started using everything they could to quietly undermine my work. 

And they're smart about it, that's the thing. It's not always loud or obvious. It's the schedule changes that always happen at the worst possible moment. It's the seating choices—like putting the second violins just far enough back that the blend is completely ruined, and then claiming it was an acoustic decision based on the hall, which is ridiculous if you know anything about the physics of sound in that specific space. It's the little comments during rehearsals, the whispers right as I raise the baton, the sighs when I ask for a section to be repeated. 

And sure, they have excuses. They always have excuses. They'll show me emails from the venue manager supposedly explaining why the chairs had to be moved, or they'll produce these little scribbled notes from the librarian about why the scores were distributed late. They have this whole paper trail of "coincidences" and "miscommunications." But I know what it really is. I've been dealing with it for two years. You don't just have that many consecutive accidents that all specifically target one person's ability to do their job. So no, I'm not wrong. I know exactly what they're doing, no matter how many emails they wave in my face to try and prove otherwise.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses absolute certainty that colleagues are sabotaging him and refuses to accept contradictory evidence (emails, notes), indicating a fixed persecutory delusion.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had times when your thoughts felt jumbled or hard to follow, or other people said you were making little sense?
turns.patient_response:
Jumbled? Hard to follow? No, not at all. I mean, honestly, I think I'm probably the most articulate person in that entire building. When I'm on the podium, my instructions have to be incredibly precise. I have to communicate complex musical ideas—timbre, phrasing, articulation—to sixty different people simultaneously. If my thoughts were jumbled, the music would fall apart instantly. And it doesn't. When I can actually get them to play, when they aren't actively trying to ruin the rehearsal, the music is perfectly coherent. 

I've never had anyone tell me I wasn't making sense. Well, except maybe the operations manager, but like I said, he's just playing dumb. He knows exactly what I'm saying when I point out the scheduling conflicts, he just pretends not to follow my logic so he doesn't have to deal with the ensemble's behavior. But in terms of my actual speech, my thoughts? No, I'm completely clear. I write extensive program notes, I give pre-concert lectures, I communicate constantly with the administration and the guest soloists. 

If anything, I think I'm almost too hyper-aware, too focused. I notice every single detail, every slight change in the room's dynamic, every misplaced stand, every whispered comment. My mind is constantly analyzing all of it, trying to stay one step ahead of whatever they're planning next. So, no, my thoughts aren't jumbled. They're just entirely occupied with trying to navigate this incredibly hostile environment they've created for me. I'm just trying to do my job, and to do that, I have to be sharper and more focused than everyone else in the room. There's no room for jumbled thoughts when you're constantly playing defense.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses clear persecutory beliefs, stating that others are 'actively trying to ruin the rehearsal' and 'planning next' in a 'hostile environment they've created for me.'
symptom_reasoning.S079: The patient describes being 'hyper-aware' and 'too focused,' noticing every detail and constantly analyzing the room to stay ahead of perceived threats.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies having jumbled thoughts or being hard to follow, stating they are completely clear and articulate.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had any other unusual beliefs or experiences outside of this situation with the ensemble?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. Like I said earlier, my life outside of this job is perfectly normal. I mean, I go home, I work on my scores, I listen to recordings, I occasionally meet up with a few friends from grad school who aren't affiliated with this particular ensemble... and everything is fine. It's completely fine. I don't walk down the street thinking people are following me, I don't think the government is tapping my phone, I don't believe in aliens or ghosts or... whatever else you might consider an "unusual belief." 

I'm a very rational, analytical person. You have to be, to do what I do. Composing and directing—it's essentially architecture with sound. It requires logic, structure, an understanding of form and proportion. I approach my whole life that way. I pay my rent on time, I go to the dentist, I buy my groceries at the same market every Sunday morning. There's absolutely nothing out of the ordinary about my day-to-day existence, except for the fact that when I step onto that podium, I am stepping into a completely manufactured, hostile environment. 

If I were the kind of person who just naturally had bizarre ideas or thought the whole world was out to get me, don't you think it would bleed into other areas of my life? I'd be having issues with my landlord, or fighting with the barista at the coffee shop, or convinced that my friends were secretly plotting against me. But none of that is happening. The only place I have any kind of conflict, the only place where I'm experiencing this... this targeted campaign, is with those specific musicians in that specific hall. So no, outside of the ensemble, my life is completely, entirely mundane. Boring, even, if you don't count the music.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient reiterates their fixed belief that the musicians are conducting a 'targeted campaign' against them in a 'manufactured, hostile environment.'
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly answers 'No, no, nothing like that' when asked about having any other unusual experiences.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient emphasizes their normal, structured daily routine (paying rent, going to the dentist, grocery shopping) and denies any out-of-the-ordinary behavior.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports continuing to engage in their usual activities (working on scores, listening to recordings) and socializing with friends, denying social withdrawal or loss of interest.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe this sabotage is part of a larger, implausible plot with an impossible or bizarre explanation, or does it still seem like a realistic workplace scheme to you?
turns.patient_response:
Implausible? Bizarre? No, no, not at all. I mean, I'm not sitting here telling you they're using mind control or, I don't know, intercepting my thoughts through the baton or something ridiculous like that. It's completely realistic. It's almost painfully realistic, which is why it's so frustrating that nobody else seems to want to acknowledge it. It's just a classic, albeit highly coordinated, workplace scheme. 

You see this kind of thing in the arts all the time, honestly. It's a very competitive field. Egos get bruised easily. I came in, I was young, I got this commission that a lot of older, more established people probably felt they deserved, or at least they felt I *didn't* deserve. And so they formed a little clique. It's just human nature, really, just taken to a very toxic extreme. They talk behind my back, they coordinate their little disruptions—the late scores, the chair shuffling, the whispered conversations right when I need the room's attention. It's all very mundane, logistical sabotage. 

There's no grand, impossible conspiracy here. It's not the Illuminati. It's just three or four bitter musicians who have decided they don't like me, they don't respect my authority on the podium, and they want to make my job as difficult as humanly possible so that I either quit or I look so incompetent that the board decides not to renew my contract. That's it. It's just petty, vindictive, coordinated workplace bullying. And the fact that they use the bureaucracy of the ensemble—the venue manager, the librarian, the operations manager—to cover their tracks just proves how realistic and grounded the whole thing is. They know exactly how to manipulate the system to make it look like a string of accidents. It's infuriating, but it's certainly not bizarre.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, detailed belief that a group of musicians is coordinating a realistic workplace scheme to sabotage their career, indicative of a persecutory delusion.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had similar suspicions that other people were trying to undermine or take advantage of you in other parts of your life, like with friends, family, or neighbors?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, not at all. Like I was saying before, this is strictly contained to the hall. It's just them. My life outside of that building is completely fine, honestly. I don't look at my neighbors and think they're stealing my mail, I don't think my friends from grad school are talking about me behind my back. I mean, my wife and I, things are basically steady at home. We have our normal routines. We cook dinner together, we watch a movie, we talk about her day... she's a graphic designer, so she has her own client issues, but it's nothing like what I'm dealing with. But between us? No suspicion, no tension, nothing like that. 

And my own work—my solitary work, I mean—is going perfectly well. Outside of this issue with the ensemble, I still meet all my deadlines for commissions. I'm keeping up with my composing. I sit at my piano in the mornings, and the ideas flow just fine. I'm not distracted by some overarching paranoia. I even still run most mornings. I get up at 6:00 AM, I run my usual four-mile loop around the park near our apartment, and I don't spend that time looking over my shoulder or wondering if the guy walking his golden retriever is secretly working for the principal cellist. 

I'm telling you, it's just this one specific group of people in this one specific context. If I were just a generally paranoid person who thought everyone was out to get me, I wouldn't be able to sit down and write a thirty-minute symphony movement, would I? I wouldn't be able to just go for a jog and enjoy the morning air. I'd be a wreck. But I'm not a wreck. I'm highly functional in every single other aspect of my life. It's only when I have to stand in front of those specific musicians, knowing what they're doing to undermine me, that there's any problem at all. My friends, my family, my wife... they're my support system. I trust them completely.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains a fixed belief that specific musicians are actively working to undermine him.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states he is not distracted by overarching paranoia and can focus well on his composing.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient continues to engage in and enjoy his daily activities, such as composing music and going for morning jogs.
symptom_reasoning.S075: The patient denies feeling detached from others, emphasizing that he completely trusts his wife, family, and friends as his support system.
symptom_reasoning.S079: The patient denies scanning for danger or looking over his shoulder while out in public.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had the feeling that people in other settings, like strangers or coworkers elsewhere, were trying to harm, monitor, or undermine you too?
turns.patient_response:
I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, Doctor, but... no. Really, no. I mean, I know we just touched on this, but I really want to be clear that strangers on the street or people in other settings are completely irrelevant to what's happening to me. 

When I go out for my run most mornings—and I do still run most mornings, usually right around 6:00 or 6:15 depending on how late I was up analyzing scores the night before—I'm just a guy in sweatpants. I see the same people in the park, you know, the guy with the golden retriever, maybe a few people commuting... I don't look at them and think they're monitoring my pace or reporting my route back to the principal oboist. That would be absurd. 

And as for other coworkers or other professional settings, it's the same thing. Because, outside of this one specific, incredibly frustrating issue with the ensemble, my career is functioning perfectly. I still meet all my deadlines for other commissions. Actually, I just turned in a completely separate string quartet piece two weeks ahead of schedule. I keep up with my composing every single day. I sit at the piano in my apartment, I work out the voicings, the counterpoint, and the music flows exactly the way it always has. Nobody is sneaking in to erase my hard drive or alter my sheet music. 

And things at home with my wife are basically steady, just like I was saying. We just go about our normal, everyday lives. She works on her graphic design layouts in the living room, I work on my orchestrations in the study, we make dinner—usually something simple, like pasta, because by the end of the day we're both pretty drained—and that's it. There's no one trying to harm me, there's no one monitoring my emails, there's no grand conspiracy in my neighborhood or at the grocery store. It is literally just that one hall, with those specific musicians, during those specific rehearsals. I don't know how else to explain that my life is incredibly, almost boringly normal everywhere else.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms ongoing persecutory beliefs regarding the principal oboist and the ensemble, even while denying that these delusions extend to strangers or other settings.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly denies failing to finish work, stating he meets all deadlines and recently turned in a piece two weeks early.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies loss of interest or motivation, maintaining his daily composing, running routine, and normal home life.
symptom_reasoning.S075: The patient denies social detachment, describing a steady, normal, and engaged daily life with his wife at home.

turns.doctor_question: Have you always been seen as unusually odd or eccentric in the way you think, dress, or relate to people, even before this rehearsal conflict started?
turns.patient_response:
Odd? Eccentric? No, not at all. I mean, look at me, look at how I dress. I'm just wearing a standard button-down shirt and slacks. When I'm working, when I'm on the podium, it's the standard black suit, maybe a dark turtleneck if we're doing a contemporary piece, but nothing flashy. I don't wear capes or, I don't know, mismatched neon socks to make some sort of avant-garde statement. I've always just dressed completely normally. 

Even back in grad school, where you definitely get those types—you know, the student composers who refuse to wear shoes in the practice rooms or who only communicate in abstract, philosophical metaphors because they think it makes them seem like misunderstood geniuses—I was never like that. I've always been very grounded. I relate to people perfectly fine. I had a solid group of friends in my master's program, we'd go out for drinks after the orchestration seminars, we'd talk about normal things, sports, movies, not just endless debates about atonality. And I met my wife during that time, and like I said, we have a very standard, steady relationship. We just get along like normal people.

If anything, I'm actually known for being very organized and pragmatic, which you absolutely have to be if you're going to direct an ensemble. You can't be some eccentric, head-in-the-clouds type and manage a tight rehearsal schedule, balance the acoustics of a difficult hall, and communicate clearly with dozens of different musicians... well, communicate clearly with the ones who aren't actively trying to sabotage you, anyway. But no, nobody has ever called me odd. If anything, I've been told by my mentors that I'm almost too analytical, too structured for a creative field. I color inside the lines, socially speaking. I always have. 

So this idea that I might be some eccentric weirdo who just naturally rubs people the wrong way because I'm out of touch with reality or because I act strangely... that's just not me. It's never been me. I'm just a regular, hard-working guy who happens to write and direct music, and who just happens to be dealing with a very specific, very vindictive group of people at work. But before this? No, completely normal. Almost boringly normal, really.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient casually mentions that musicians at work are 'actively trying to sabotage' him and describes them as a 'very vindictive group,' indicating persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly denies having trouble organizing, stating he is known for being 'very organized and pragmatic' and can 'manage a tight rehearsal schedule.'
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient denies any odd, eccentric, or disorganized behavior, emphasizing that he dresses and acts 'completely normally.'
symptom_reasoning.S075: The patient denies social detachment, noting he relates to people 'perfectly fine,' had a 'solid group of friends,' and maintains a 'standard, steady relationship' with his wife.

turns.doctor_question: If someone you trusted showed you clear proof that these incidents were accidental, would you still believe the ensemble was targeting you?
turns.patient_response:
Look, the thing about "clear proof" is... well, what even constitutes proof in a situation like this? Because they actually *have* tried to show me things. I mean, that's really the whole crux of it, that's why I'm here talking to you today. Because for almost two years now—ever since that big commission, which honestly should have been a massive high point in my career, something to celebrate—I’ve just been completely unable to shake this absolute certainty about what they're doing. 

It’s a few specific people in the ensemble, and they’ve been using all these incredibly subtle tactics to quietly undermine my work. And they are subtle, which is what makes it so maddening. I'm talking about sudden schedule changes that just happen to conflict with when I need the hall, or very deliberate seating choices that completely mess with the acoustics and the balance I'm trying to build for a piece, and then these... these little comments in rehearsals. Just under their breath, or phrased as innocent questions about the tempo or the bowing, but they aren't innocent. They're designed to make the rest of the players doubt my direction.

And the frustrating part, to your question about proof, is that they *do* produce these so-called explanations. When I call them out on it, they'll forward me emails or pull up notes from the administration or the stage manager that supposedly explain why the seating had to change or why the rehearsal time was bumped. They wave these printouts in my face like, "See? It's just an administrative error, the hall was double-booked, look at this memo!" 

So even when they show me these emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away as some big string of harmless accidents, it doesn't change anything for me. I can't just turn off what I know is happening. If someone I trusted, like my wife, looked at those same emails... I mean, she might think it looks like an accident on paper, sure, because these musicians are very careful about how they document things. They know how to cover their tracks. But paper doesn't capture the tone of those little comments in the hall, does it? An email doesn't capture the smirks when I have to stop the rehearsal to fix a seating arrangement they purposely messed up. 

So, no, even with their "proof," I wouldn't change my mind. I can't shake the certainty. It's been two years of this constant, quiet sabotage since the commission. You just don't have two solid years of perfectly timed "accidents" that only ever seem to negatively impact my time on the podium.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly states they have an absolute certainty that ensemble members are quietly undermining their work, and that even when presented with documentary proof to the contrary, they refuse to change their mind, indicating a fixed false belief.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever fear that these people might physically harm you or attack you?
turns.patient_response:
Physical harm? Like... like actually attack me? Oh, no. No, no, no. I mean, I can see why you might ask that, given how intense and stressful this whole situation is, but no, I've never once worried about my physical safety. 

I mean, think about who we're talking about here. These aren't street thugs or mobsters, Doctor. They are conservatory-trained, highly educated classical musicians. Can you even imagine it? The principal cellist waiting for me in the alley behind the concert hall with a lead pipe? Or the woodwind section jumping me in the parking garage? It’s... well, it’s almost comical to even picture it. That is just not how these people operate. 

If they were to physically attack me, there would be police involved, they’d be arrested, they’d immediately lose their chairs, and they’d be blacklisted from every major symphony and chamber group in the country. They are far, far too calculating for something as crude and obvious as physical violence. 

Their weapons are entirely professional and, frankly, psychological. Like I was saying before, it’s all about the seating arrangements, the whispers, the perfectly timed missed cues, the union grievances over three extra minutes of rehearsal time. Why would they risk a physical altercation—which would instantly prove me right to the administration and vindicate everything I've been saying, by the way—when they can just ruin a recording session by deliberately dragging the tempo in the third movement so subtly that the producers blame *me* for poor pacing? 

That’s what they want. They want to dismantle my reputation. They want to undermine my authority on the podium and make it look like I'm incompetent, not break my legs. So, no, I walk to my car after a late rehearsal perfectly fine. I don't look over my shoulder for muggers or attackers. I just... I just brace myself for whatever administrative nightmare or acoustic sabotage they've decided to spring on me the next morning. But physical danger? No, never.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, detailed belief that the musicians are actively conspiring to sabotage their career, ruin their reputation, and undermine their authority, which is indicative of persecutory delusions.

turns.doctor_question: Is there any part of you that thinks you might be mistaken about the ensemble sabotaging you?
turns.patient_response:
Mistaken? You mean... do I ever wake up and think, 'Oh, maybe I'm just overthinking all of this?' No. I really don't. And I know I touched on this a moment ago, but it really is the entire reason I'm here talking to you. Because for almost two years now—literally right after that commission was announced, which again, should have been the best time of my life—I’ve been completely unable to shake the certainty of what's happening. 

I wish there was a part of me that thought I was mistaken, I really do! It would be so much easier if I was just imagining things. But when you are the one standing on the podium, day in and day out, you see it. You feel the shift in the room. It’s just a few people in the ensemble, but they are so relentless. Like I was saying, they started using these specific tactics—the sudden schedule changes, the bizarre seating choices that completely throw off the balance of the string section, and those little comments in rehearsals... they use all of it to quietly undermine my work. 

And even when they do what I mentioned before, you know, even when they show me those emails or the stage manager's notes that supposedly explain it all away as some innocent administrative error... it doesn't make me doubt myself for a second. It actually just reinforces what I know is happening, because I see how much effort they put into creating this perfect little paper trail to cover their tracks. You don't just imagine that level of coordination. So, no, I'm not mistaken. I'm absolutely certain.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses absolute certainty that ensemble members are sabotaging them and maintains this belief without doubt even when presented with contradictory evidence like emails or notes.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever believed that ordinary events or coincidences have a special personal meaning just for you?
turns.patient_response:
Special personal meaning? I'm... I'm not sure I completely follow what you're asking. Like, do you mean seeing a certain number on a license plate and thinking it's a message from the universe? Or seeing a bird fly by and thinking it's a sign about how my next performance is going to go? 

If that's what you mean, then no. No, absolutely not. I don't look at random, ordinary occurrences and think they're somehow about me. I mean, if it rains, it rains. If someone drops a coffee cup in the conservatory lobby, it's just a dropped coffee cup. I'm actually a very grounded, highly analytical person. You really have to be, in my line of work. When you're composing or directing an orchestra, you are dealing with structure, with form, with incredibly precise mathematical relationships between notes and rhythms and time signatures.
